doc.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Columbia drops him in 1971
summary: His lawyers learn Columbia dropped him six months earlier; he and Tony Bennett were then invited to play at the Columbia meeting.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Let me focus on 1971. Columbia starts going through turmoil. They’re changing their roster. They’re moving away from a lot of the jazz acts, and your contract is terminated at that point. How did that happen? What were your reactions? Why did that happen?
It’s a strange thing. I didn’t know that I had been terminated. No-one told me. I forget how I finally found out.
Jim Bancroft came to negotiate a new deal. He called up the business [?].

The attorneys came to negotiate, because it was time to renew the contract. Every year it had been renewed just sort of automatically. No-one even talked about it. It just renewed. So when they said that their business, the reason they had come, was to negotiate Dave’s next contract, then they said, “Oh, there’s nothing to negotiate. We’ve dropped him.”
There was another artist they dropped at the same time too, which proved a very funny story.

I will sell that story. There was a world meeting of – Columbia representatives from every part of the world were meeting in New York. They request who they’d like to hear of their artists. It’s usually someone that they’ve done business with for years and is doing well. That’s who would entertain at their gathering. So Goddard Lieberson, then president of Columbia, called me and said, “Could you come in and play for the Columbia meeting.” I said, “I’m no longer – I’ve been dropped from your company.” See, he’d been kicked upstairs and Clive Davis, I think, was moved in to be president. Goddard was running the Yankees – the baseball team – a children’s store . . .
A conglomerate of industries. But Clive Davis was the head of the record.

So I got to the meeting. Everybody’s glad to see me, like they have been for years. I see Tony Bennett. I say hello. I said, “Tony, I don’t belong here.” He said, “Why?” I said, “They’ve dropped me, and yet Goddard has begged me to come and play.” He said, “They’ve dropped me too, and Goddard asked me to come.” So here are the guys that have dropped. I’ll tell you, we had done a good job for Columbia over the years.
And still do. Those recordings still sell in huge numbers.

I remember seeing Tony go through a low period, and then, because of his son or something, to get back to Columbia and just go sky-high in sales. He’s still doing it. I could be doing it too, but there’s problems [ ]. I’m still with the label, but no agreements or anything. They’re mostly sending out my old records and repackaging them, instead of – they should be doing new things if they want to keep up to date with me. But I have three other companies now, Telarc, Concord, and old Fantasy, all under one big company. So I’m doing fine, but I’m not doing what I should be doing with SONY Legacy.
